definition: In mathematics, an interval contractor (or contractor for short) associated to a set X {\displaystyle X} is an operator C {\displaystyle C} which associates to a hyperrectangle [ x ] {\displaystyle [x]} in R n {\displaystyle {\mathbf {R}}^{n}} another box C ( [ x ] ) {\displaystyle C([x])} of R n {\displaystyle {\mathbf {R}}^{n}} such that the two following properties are always satisfied: C ( [ x ] ) ⊂ [ x ] {\displaystyle C([x])\subset [x]} (contractance property) C ( [ x ] ) ∩ X = [ x ] ∩ X {\displaystyle C([x])\cap X=[x]\cap X} (completeness property) A contractor associated to a constraint (such as an equation or an inequality) is a contractor associated to the set X {\displaystyle X} of all x {\displaystyle x} which satisfy the constraint.
details: Contractors make it possible to improve the efficiency of branch-and-bound algorithms classically used in interval analysis.

explainer.lead: An interval contractor is an operator that maps a hyperrectangle to a smaller box while preserving its intersection with a target set. It matters because contractors improve the efficiency of branch-and-bound algorithms used in interval analysis.

tiers.eli5: Think of trimming a rough box down to the part that could still contain the answer, without cutting away anything that might be inside.
tiers.practitioner: Numerical and interval-analysis engineers apply contractors to tighten boxes before branching, reducing search effort. A pitfall is expecting contraction to solve the problem alone; it narrows boxes but does not itself find the solution.
tiers.paperLevel: For a set X, a contractor C associates to a hyperrectangle [x] in R^n another box C([x]) such that C([x]) is a subset of [x] (contractance) and C([x]) intersect X equals [x] intersect X (consistency). Limits: it preserves the intersection with X but may not shrink a box at all.

explainer.example: Given a box known to contain a solution, the contractor returns a smaller box that still contains every point of the solution set inside the original box.
